This module lists frequently observed mistakes, bugs, and anti-patterns seen in everyday memory leaks work, so they can be recognized and avoided during typical memory leaks tasks.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Keep memory leaks changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
2. Keep memory leaks outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
3. Check that memory leaks terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
4. Prefer the simplest memory leaks approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
5. Re-check edge cases relevant to memory leaks (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
6. Measure before optimizing any memory leaks bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
7. State assumptions about memory leaks explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
8. Document any non-obvious memory leaks decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
9. Surface known limitations of a chosen memory leaks approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
10. When memory leaks guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not apply generic memory leaks advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Do not skip documenting memory leaks assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of memory leaks correctness.
- Do not silently drop memory leaks edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Avoid introducing new memory leaks abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.

CLOSING NOTE
Revisit these memory leaks guidelines if the task's constraints change significantly during the work.
